opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's a really important distinction, and people often blur the two.

The first role, acceleration, is where AI is already delivering a lot of value today. A scientist has a hypothesis or a direction, and AI helps them get there faster. It might be screening millions of candidate molecules instead of a few hundred, running a surrogate model instead of a week-long simulation, or reading and summarizing thousands of papers so the researcher doesn't miss something relevant. The human still defines the question, decides what matters, and interprets the result. AI compresses the time and cost of each loop in the scientific process. That's enormously valuable, because in many fields the bottleneck really is iteration speed. If you can go from one experiment cycle a month to one a day, the whole field moves differently.

The second role, discovery, is more ambitious and more subtle. Here we're asking whether AI can find something genuinely new that humans weren't looking for: a new mechanism, a new material class, a pattern in the data that suggests a law we didn't know existed. Discovery isn't just doing the same search faster. It involves choosing which question to ask, recognizing when a result is surprising rather than just noisy, and connecting it to a broader explanatory framework. That's the part of science that has traditionally relied on intuition and taste.

Where I think it gets interesting is that the boundary is moving. When acceleration gets dramatic enough, it starts to look like discovery. If you can explore a space so thoroughly that you hit regions no human would have thought to try, you can stumble into genuinely novel results. Some of the protein structure and materials work in the last few years has that flavor. But I'd still be careful about calling that "AI making discoveries" in the full sense, because a human usually had to recognize why the result mattered.

So my practical framing is this: today, AI is a very powerful accelerator and an increasingly capable collaborator in discovery. The real test of discovery is whether the system can propose a hypothesis, design the experiment to test it, interpret an unexpected outcome, and update its understanding, closing the loop more or less on its own. We're seeing early pieces of that with autonomous labs and agent-style systems, but closing that loop reliably, with the judgment to know what's important, is still the frontier. That's where I think the next few years will be most exciting.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes AI speeding up a human-directed process from AI generating genuinely new knowledge humans were not seeking.

r002.rationale: It discusses AI as a collaborator and mentions autonomous labs, but does not compare a co-scientist AI workbench to an integrated development environment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it helps to be honest about where the field actually is right now. Most of what we call AI for Science today is in the first category: acceleration. It's AI as a very capable assistant. It reads the literature faster than you can, it writes the boilerplate code for your simulation, it helps you clean up a dataset, it suggests which experiment to run next out of a space of options you already defined. That's tremendously valuable. If you ask a graduate student how much of their week is spent on things that are not thinking, the answer is usually most of it. Compressing that is real progress, and it compounds.

But I'd draw the line like this. In acceleration, the scientist still owns the question. The hypothesis, the framing, the sense of what's interesting, all of that comes from a person, and the AI makes the loop from question to answer shorter. In discovery, the system contributes something to the question itself, or finds a result that nobody was looking for. AlphaFold is the example everyone cites, and it's a good one, but notice the problem was posed by humans over fifty years. The model solved it brilliantly, but it didn't decide that protein structure mattered.

Coming from experimental physics, the thing I keep in mind is that discovery usually happens where the model of the world breaks. When we first saw superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene, it wasn't because a tool told us to look there. It was a strange signal that didn't fit, and a willingness to take the anomaly seriously rather than treat it as noise. Current AI systems are, by construction, very good at the regime where the data is dense and the patterns are known. Discovery lives in the sparse regime, where you have three weird data points and a hunch.

So the real test for whether AI is making discoveries, rather than accelerating them, is whether it can generate a hypothesis that a good scientist would find surprising and then turn out to be right. We're starting to see glimpses of that in narrow domains, materials, some areas of chemistry. But I'd say the honest framing is that we're in a long acceleration phase, and the acceleration is itself going to change what discovery looks like, because when experiments get cheap, you can afford to chase a lot more hunches.

r001.rationale: The response draws the line at whether the AI contributes to the question or finds an unanticipated result, distinguishing that from shortening a scientist-led question-to-answer loop.

r002.rationale: It does not liken a co-scientist AI workbench to an integrated development environment for scientific work.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish between making an existing research process more efficient and changing what we can discover. In the first case, scientists already know the question and broadly know how to approach it. AI might help analyze data, run simulations, or screen candidates. You get an answer faster, or at a lower cost, but the basic scientific framework stays the same.

Discovery goes a step further: can AI help identify a pattern we hadn’t noticed, suggest a hypothesis we wouldn’t have considered, or reveal where our existing explanation breaks down? The important point is that producing a prediction isn’t automatically making a scientific discovery. We still need to test it and understand what the evidence actually establishes.

But these two roles aren’t separate boxes. If you make a calculation a thousand times faster, you may suddenly be able to explore a space that was previously inaccessible. That improvement in efficiency can create the conditions for discovery. So I’d ask both: does AI help us do familiar science faster, and does it enable us to ask questions we couldn’t meaningfully investigate before?

r001.rationale: The response contrasts making an existing research process more efficient with discovery that identifies unnoticed patterns, proposes new hypotheses, or challenges existing explanations.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a co-scientist AI workbench or compare one to an integrated development environment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are two different levels of contribution. At the first level, scientists already know what question they want to ask, and AI helps them answer it faster. It might help analyze data, run simulations, or search through possible materials. The scientific workflow is still largely defined by people; AI reduces the time and cost of carrying it out.

Discovery goes a step further. Can AI help us identify a pattern we weren’t looking for, propose a hypothesis we hadn’t considered, or suggest an experiment that changes our understanding? In that case, it contributes to deciding what questions to ask, as well as how to answer them.

But the boundary isn’t sharp. If you make a calculation a thousand times faster, you may suddenly be able to explore a regime that was previously inaccessible. An improvement in efficiency can create the conditions for a discovery.

The key, to me, is validation. An unexpected AI output is a candidate for a discovery. You still need evidence, experiments, and a clear understanding of where the result holds. So I would distinguish the two by asking: did AI help us do an existing task better, or did it help us establish something new about the world?

r001.rationale: It distinguishes AI speeding up a scientist’s existing task from helping formulate questions or establish something new about the world.

r002.rationale: It does not compare a co-scientist AI workbench to an integrated development environment.
